title: HE CALLED A DEAD MAN BY NAME
paragraphs:
HE CALLED A DEAD MAN BY NAME
The Astonishing Depth Behind the Raising of Lazarus—and What It Means for Every Heart That Feels Beyond Hope
There are moments in Scripture that do more than inform the mind.
They confront the soul.

They pull back the curtain between heaven and earth and allow us to witness something so profound that even after thousands of years, humanity still finds itself standing in stunned silence before it.
The raising of Lazarus is one of those moments.
Most people know the story.
A man dies.
Jesus arrives late.
A miracle happens.
Lazarus walks out of the tomb.
But beneath the familiar narrative lies a depth so breathtaking that many believers have never fully explored it.
This is not merely a story about resurrection.
It is a revelation of who Jesus Christ truly is.
It is a story about grief, disappointment, waiting, divine timing, spiritual death, eternal life, and the God who specializes in rewriting endings.
It is a story that begins with a scandal and ends with grace.
And perhaps that is why it still resonates so deeply today.
Because every one of us knows what it feels like to stand before a tomb.
Not always a physical one.
Sometimes it is a broken marriage.
A shattered dream.
An addiction.
A prodigal child.
A ruined reputation.
A secret sin.
A faith that feels buried beneath disappointment.
The story of Lazarus is God's declaration that no tomb is too sealed, no situation too hopeless, and no heart too far gone for Jesus Christ.
The account is found in John 11.
Lazarus lived in Bethany with his sisters Martha and Mary.
The family shared a close relationship with Jesus.
John 11:5 specifically tells us:
"Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus."
This detail matters.
Because what happens next appears contradictory.
Lazarus becomes gravely ill.
His sisters send an urgent message:
"Lord, behold, he whom You love is sick."
Yet Jesus does not immediately go.
Instead, He remains where He is for two additional days.
To human eyes, it looks like neglect.
To grieving hearts, it looks like silence.
To Martha and Mary, it likely felt like abandonment.
How many believers know that feeling?
The prayer was sincere.
The need was real.
The situation was urgent.
Yet heaven seemed silent.
The answer did not come when expected.
The miracle did not arrive on schedule.
The breakthrough was delayed.
But John records something remarkable.
Jesus said:
"This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God."
The delay was not rejection.
It was preparation.
Sometimes God's apparent absence is actually His deeper involvement.
What feels like divine silence may be the stage upon which divine glory is about to be revealed.
By the time Jesus arrives, Lazarus has been dead four days.
This detail is extraordinarily important.
In Jewish understanding during the period, many believed the soul lingered near the body for three days after death before departing completely.
Whether accurate or not, the cultural belief matters because John intentionally emphasizes four days.
Lazarus was unquestionably dead.
No misunderstanding.
No possibility of recovery.
No chance of human explanation.
The situation had moved beyond hope.
Exactly where Jesus intended to reveal His glory.
Martha meets Jesus and says:
"Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died."
There is pain in those words.
Faith mixed with disappointment.
Trust wrestling with grief.
Belief colliding with reality.
Many Christians have prayed versions of the same sentence.
"Lord, if You had acted sooner..."
"Lord, if You had answered differently..."
"Lord, if You had intervened..."
Yet Jesus responds with one of the most profound declarations ever spoken.
In Greek, He says:
"Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē."
"I am the resurrection and the life."
The phrase Egō eimi (ἐγώ εἰμι) means "I AM."
This echoes God's self-revelation in Exodus.
In Hebrew, God revealed Himself to Moses as:

אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה
(Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh)
"I AM WHO I AM."
(Exodus 3:14)
Jesus is not merely claiming the ability to resurrect.
He is claiming divine identity.
He is not saying resurrection is something He performs.
He is declaring resurrection is something He is.
Life itself stands before Martha.
The One who authored existence is speaking to a grieving sister.
Then comes one of the most astonishing verses in all Scripture.
John 11:35.
The shortest verse in most English translations.
"Jesus wept."
In Greek:

ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς
(Edakrysen ho Iēsous)
"Jesus shed tears."
Think carefully about this moment.
Jesus knows what He is about to do.
He knows Lazarus will walk out of the tomb.
He knows resurrection is moments away.
Yet He still weeps.
Why?
Because God is not indifferent to human suffering.
The tears of Jesus reveal the heart of God.
He is not emotionally detached from pain.
He enters into it.
He stands beside mourners.
He feels the weight of loss.
He understands heartbreak.
He knows grief from the inside.
This is one reason Christianity transformed the world.
In Jesus, we do not find a distant deity observing suffering from afar.
We find Emmanuel.
God with us.
God among us.
God weeping with us.
Then comes the command.
"Take away the stone."
Martha hesitates.
In the King James Version she says:
"Lord, by this time he stinketh."
The reality of death had become undeniable.
Decay had already begun.
The miracle appeared impossible.
Yet Jesus orders the stone removed.
Then He cries out:
"Lazarus, come forth!"
Many pastors throughout church history have noted an intriguing truth.
Jesus called Lazarus by name.
Had He merely shouted "Come forth," every grave might have emptied.
Whether taken literally or illustratively, the point remains powerful.
The voice that created the universe now addresses one dead man.
And death obeys.
Lazarus emerges.
Still wrapped in grave clothes.
Alive.
Breathing.
Restored.
But another detail is often overlooked.
Jesus says:
"Loose him, and let him go."
The miracle of life had occurred.
Yet the grave clothes still needed removal.
How many believers have experienced this?
Saved by Christ.
Made alive spiritually.
Yet still carrying remnants of old habits, old wounds, old fears, old identities.
Resurrection is immediate.
Transformation is often progressive.
Jesus raises us from death.
Then He patiently removes the grave clothes.
The story of Lazarus is not merely historical.
It is prophetic.
It points directly toward the greater resurrection soon to come.
Because Lazarus would eventually die again.
His miracle was temporary.
Jesus' resurrection would be permanent.
Lazarus came out of a tomb.
Jesus left one forever.
Lazarus was called by another.
Jesus rose by His own authority.
Lazarus was raised.
Jesus is the Resurrection.
This distinction changes everything.
The raising of Lazarus serves as the final and greatest sign before Christ's own crucifixion.
Ironically, the miracle that displayed His glory also accelerated the plot against Him.
John 11:53 records that many religious leaders intensified their plans to kill Jesus.
The raising of Lazarus became part of the road to Calvary.
The miracle that gave life to one man contributed to the death sentence of another.
Yet this too was grace.
Because Jesus would willingly enter the ultimate tomb so that sinners could walk out of theirs.
He would bear our sin.
Carry our shame.
Endure our judgment.
Conquer our death.
And offer eternal life freely to all who believe.
This is why the story remains so deeply personal.
Because every reader eventually discovers that Lazarus is not merely a character in the narrative.
He is a mirror.
We were spiritually dead.
Paul writes in Ephesians that we were "dead in trespasses and sins."
Dead people cannot save themselves.
Dead people cannot resurrect themselves.
Dead people need a Savior.
And Jesus still calls names.
Not only Lazarus.
Yours.
Mine.
The addict.
The skeptic.
The hypocrite.
The prodigal.
The ashamed.
The broken.
The exhausted.
The one who thinks God could never forgive them.
The voice that echoed through Bethany still speaks today.
And when Christ calls, death loses its grip.
Perhaps that is why this story continues to move hearts centuries later.
Because every person longs for the possibility that their tomb is not the end.
That their failure is not final.
That their scandal does not get the last word.
That grace is stronger than shame.
That Jesus can still rewrite what appears irreversible.
And that is exactly what He does.
The raising of Lazarus reveals a Savior who is never late, even when He seems delayed.
A Savior who weeps with the hurting.
A Savior who calls dead things to life.
A Savior who transforms graves into testimonies.
A Savior who turns scandal into grace.
What "tomb" has Jesus brought you out of?
Your testimony may become someone else's reason to keep believing.
The stone was never the end of the story—only the place where heaven began rewriting it.
